solution.concept_anchor: NWDA establishment year and nodal ministry
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because K.L. Rao is strongly associated with the interlinking idea, leading students to assume he also established the institutional body.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): K.L. Rao proposed the Ganga-Cauvery link concept in 1972 — he did not establish NWDA.
Eliminate (c): NWDA was not established in 1990; it was constituted in 1982.
Eliminate (d): Captain Dastur proposed the Garland Canal, an alternative conceptual proposal — he had no role in founding NWDA.
Confirm (b): NWDA was established in 1982 under the Ministry of Water Resources (now Jal Shakti) to carry out surveys and prepare feasibility reports for interlinking links.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who associate K.L. Rao's 1972 Ganga-Cauvery proposal with the formal institutional beginning of river interlinking tend to conflate conceptual origin with institutional establishment. NWDA was set up a decade later in 1982 as a registered society — not as a statutory body — specifically to carry forward the technical groundwork. The entity-swap trap here places K.L. Rao or Dastur as the institutional founder, exploiting the confusion between the idea-givers and the agency that operationalised the agenda.
solution.final_explanation:
The National Water Development Agency (NWDA) is the nodal technical body responsible for surveys, investigations, and preparation of feasibility/DPR reports for river interlinking links under the National Perspective Plan.

• Option (a): Incorrect. K.L. Rao proposed the Ganga-Cauvery link in 1972 — a conceptual vision — but he did not establish NWDA.
• Option (b): Correct. NWDA was established in 1982 as a registered society under the then Ministry of Water Resources (now Ministry of Jal Shakti).
• Option (c): Incorrect. The year 1990 is a temporal distractor; NWDA was constituted in 1982.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Captain Dastur proposed the Garland Canal concept — an alternative to NWDA's framework — but had no role in its founding.

Value Addition:
• NWDA is a registered society, NOT a statutory body — it cannot enforce interstate agreements.
• The National Perspective Plan (NPP) under which NWDA operates has two components: Himalayan (14 links) and Peninsular (16 links).
• NWDA prepares DPRs; actual implementation is the responsibility of state governments or designated agencies.

solution.concept_anchor: Ken-Betwa Link — Peninsular component classification

statement_analysis.statement: Ken and Betwa are both tributaries of the Yamuna river.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Ken and Betwa originate in central India and drain northward to join the Yamuna, providing the hydrological basis for the link.

statement_analysis.statement: The Ken-Betwa Link Project is classified under the Himalayan Rivers Development Component of the National Perspective Plan.
statement_analysis.reason: Despite being geographically located in central India (Vindhyan region), Ken-Betwa falls under the Peninsular Rivers Development Component, not the Himalayan component.

statement_analysis.statement: The Daudhan Dam, the key storage structure of the Ken-Betwa project, involves submergence of a part of Panna Tiger Reserve.
statement_analysis.reason: The Daudhan Dam site lies within the Panna Tiger Reserve in Madhya Pradesh, creating a major biodiversity-versus-development conflict.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because students who know Ken-Betwa is in central/Vindhyan India incorrectly assume it must belong to the Himalayan component, making them doubt statements 1 and 3 and accept statement 2.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Ken and Betwa both drain into the Yamuna — this is a standard geographic fact; Statement 1 is correct.
Examine Statement 2 carefully: Ken-Betwa is in Bundelkhand/Vindhyan region, but the National Perspective Plan classifies it under the Peninsular component — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Daudhan Dam submergence affecting Panna Tiger Reserve is well-documented — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The core trap here is geographic conflation: students associate 'Himalayan component' with rivers originating in or near the Himalayan belt and 'Peninsular component' with rivers south of the Vindhyas. Ken-Betwa, being in the Vindhyan/Bundelkhand region of central India, seems misplaced in the Peninsular component. However, the National Perspective Plan's classification follows the hydrological and basin characteristics, not strictly the physiographic location. This is a classic UPSC trap where geographic intuition misleads a partially prepared candidate.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ken-Betwa Link is India's first river interlinking project to receive Cabinet approval (2021) and is at an advanced stage of implementation. Understanding its correct classification within the National Perspective Plan is critical.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Both Ken and Betwa are Yamuna tributaries, making their interlinking an intra-basin transfer within the Ganga system — a key hydrological rationale.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Despite being located in Bundelkhand (central India), Ken-Betwa is classified under the Peninsular Rivers Development Component of the NPP, not the Himalayan component. The distinction is based on the nature of rivers (non-perennial, rain-fed) rather than strict geographic location.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Daudhan Dam is proposed inside Panna Tiger Reserve in Madhya Pradesh, making this project a flashpoint for biodiversity-versus-development debate.

Value Addition:
• MoU between Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh for Ken-Betwa was signed in 2005.
• The project is estimated to provide irrigation to drought-prone Bundelkhand and Sagar districts.
• Panna Tiger Reserve hosts the critically important tiger reintroduction programme initiated in 2009.

solution.concept_anchor: NRLP primary objectives — irrigation over hydropower

statement_analysis.statement: Hydropower generation is the primary objective of the National River Linking Project.
statement_analysis.reason: Hydropower generation is a co-benefit of NRLP; the primary objectives are irrigation expansion and flood control — not power generation.

statement_analysis.statement: The projected additional irrigation potential under NRLP is approximately 35 million hectares.
statement_analysis.reason: NWDA's estimates project approximately 35 million hectares of additional irrigation as the principal benefit of the full NRLP implementation.

statement_analysis.statement: The estimated hydropower generation potential under NRLP, as projected, exceeds 50,000 MW.
statement_analysis.reason: The projected hydropower generation is approximately 34,000 MW — not exceeding 50,000 MW; the inflated figure is a scope-extension distractor.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who recall that hydropower is a benefit (which is true) and that irrigation figures are large may incorrectly flag Statement 2 as also incorrect, choosing (b).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Irrigation and flood control are the primary objectives; hydropower is explicitly a co-benefit — Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: 35 million hectares is the standard NWDA projection for additional irrigation — Statement 2 is correct, so it cannot be the answer.
Evaluate Statement 3: The projected figure is ~34,000 MW, not exceeding 50,000 MW — Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are incorrect — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The primary trap is the misidentification of hydropower as NRLP's principal objective. Because hydropower is frequently highlighted in media coverage of dam projects, students associate large water infrastructure with power generation. The UPSC tests whether candidates know that NRLP's design priority is irrigation followed by flood control, with hydropower as a secondary dividend. The inflated 50,000 MW figure in Statement 3 is a scope-extension trap on top of that, making both statements simultaneously wrong for different reasons.
solution.final_explanation:
The National River Linking Project is fundamentally an irrigation and flood management initiative, not a power project — a distinction the UPSC has repeatedly tested.

• Statement 1 — NOT Correct: Hydropower (~34,000 MW projected) is a co-benefit of NRLP, not its primary goal. Irrigation (~35 million hectares) and flood moderation are the stated primary objectives.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 35 million hectares irrigation projection is consistent with NWDA's officially published estimates.
• Statement 3 — NOT Correct: The projected hydropower is approximately 34,000 MW — stating it exceeds 50,000 MW is a numerical exaggeration.

Value Addition:
• NRLP's original cost estimate was ~₹5.6 lakh crore at 2002 prices; current estimates exceed ₹10 lakh crore.
• Navigation improvement is also listed as a tertiary benefit alongside hydropower.
• Economists have critiqued the cost-benefit ratio, arguing groundwater augmentation may be more cost-effective for water-deficit regions.

solution.concept_anchor: Himalayan component links and geopolitical dependencies

statement_analysis.statement: Kosi-Mechi link — falls under the Himalayan Rivers Development Component
statement_analysis.reason: Kosi-Mechi is one of the 14 identified links under the Himalayan component, designed to transfer Kosi flood surplus westward.

statement_analysis.statement: Himalayan component reservoirs on Ganga tributaries require cooperation from Nepal — geopolitical sensitivity
statement_analysis.reason: Major proposed storage reservoirs on Kosi, Gandak, and Ghaghra tributaries require land and treaty arrangements involving Nepal.

statement_analysis.statement: The Himalayan component is considered less complex than the Peninsular component due to perennial river flows
statement_analysis.reason: Perennial flow is an advantage for water availability but the Himalayan component is MORE complex due to transboundary rivers, seismic zone concerns, and geopolitical dependencies — not less complex.

statement_analysis.statement: Flood control in Bihar and eastern India is an explicit dual objective of the Himalayan component
statement_analysis.reason: The Himalayan component is designed with the dual purpose of irrigation augmentation and flood moderation in Bihar and eastern India.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who correctly identify that perennial flow is an advantage may still mistakenly conclude the Himalayan component is 'less complex overall,' accepting Statement 3 as correct and choosing three correct pairs.
elimination_logic: Assess pair 1: Kosi-Mechi is a standard Himalayan component link — correct.
Assess pair 2: Nepal cooperation is required for Himalayan reservoir construction — correct.
Assess pair 3: Perennial flow is an advantage, but the Himalayan component is MORE complex (not less) due to geopolitics and seismicity — incorrect.
Assess pair 4: Dual purpose (irrigation + flood control) is an explicit design feature of the Himalayan component — correct.
Three pairs are correct — select option (c) — wait, options are Only one/Only two/Only three/All four. Three correct = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 3 is a reversed-reasoning distractor: perennial flow is a genuine advantage of Himalayan rivers, and a partially prepared student may conflate 'hydrologically advantageous' with 'less complex overall.' However, complexity in the Himalayan component arises from transboundary dimensions (Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh), seismic zone risks, and difficult terrain — not from water availability. This partial truth makes Statement 3 feel plausible.
solution.final_explanation:
The Himalayan Rivers Development Component comprises 14 link proposals, primarily designed to harness flood surplus from rivers like Kosi, Gandak, and Ghaghra and route it to water-deficit areas in western and peninsular India, while simultaneously moderating floods in Bihar.

• Pair 1 — Correct: Kosi-Mechi is a confirmed Himalayan component link.
• Pair 2 — Correct: Nepal's territory is indispensable for reservoir construction on Kosi, Gandak, and Ghaghra tributaries.
• Pair 3 — Incorrect: Despite perennial flows, the Himalayan component is considered MORE complex than the Peninsular component due to transboundary geopolitics, active seismic zones, and terrain challenges.
• Pair 4 — Correct: Flood moderation in Bihar alongside irrigation is an explicit dual objective.

Value Addition:
• Bhutan's cooperation is also needed for storage on some eastern Himalayan tributaries.
• China's upstream dam projects on the Brahmaputra (Zangmu, Motuo) complicate India's surplus water calculations.
• The Himalayan component depends on large storage reservoirs — the Peninsular component relies more on run-of-river and existing reservoirs.

solution.concept_anchor: Peninsular backbone links and project nodes
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know Polavaram is on the Godavari may correctly match A-2 but then incorrectly place the Ken-Betwa component under the Himalayan component (C-4 instead of C-3), leading to option (a).
elimination_logic: Match A: Polavaram is a multipurpose project on the Godavari — it serves as a critical NODE for the Peninsular cascade — matches 2.
Match B: The Par-Tapi-Narmada link is designed to meet water needs of North Gujarat and Saurashtra — matches 4.
Match C: Ken-Betwa is classified under the Peninsular component despite being in Vindhyan/central India — matches 3.
Match D: The Mahanadi-Godavari-Krishna-Cauvery cascade is the backbone of the Peninsular Rivers Development Component — matches 1; option (c) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The key trap involves Ken-Betwa (List I item C). Students familiar with the Vindhyan geography of Ken-Betwa tend to associate it with the Himalayan component and may match it to item 4 (Himalayan component). This causes a cascade of wrong matches. Similarly, students may confuse Polavaram's role — it is a multipurpose project that acts as a node for future interlinking, not itself an interlinking project.
solution.final_explanation:
The Peninsular Rivers Development Component involves 16 links, with the Mahanadi-Godavari-Krishna-Cauvery cascade as its backbone. Key nodes and sub-links must be correctly associated.

• A-2: Polavaram on the Godavari is declared a National Project and serves as the critical node from which surplus Godavari waters would be transferred southward. It is NOT itself an interlinking project.
• B-4: Par-Tapi-Narmada link is designed to divert west-flowing Western Ghats rivers eastward to serve North Gujarat and Saurashtra's deficit regions.
• C-3: Ken-Betwa, despite being in the Vindhyan/Bundelkhand region, is classified under the Peninsular component — not the Himalayan component.
• D-1: The Mahanadi-Godavari-Krishna-Cauvery cascade is the foundational backbone of the Peninsular component, involving a chain of reservoirs transferring flood surplus southward.

Value Addition:
• Andhra Pradesh's bifurcation in 2014 created new complications for the Godavari-Krishna sharing arrangements.
• Polavaram's submergence affects tribal areas in Andhra Pradesh, making it a contested project.
• The cascading transfer concept means each river in the chain acts as both a recipient and a donor.

solution.concept_anchor: Entry 56 Union List — Parliament's authority over inter-state rivers
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both facts to be true often assume R explains A, missing the nuance that Article 262 governs dispute resolution specifically, not the legislative competence for interlinking.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? Entry 56 of the Union List empowers Parliament to regulate and develop inter-state rivers in the public interest — A is factually correct.
Step 2 — Is R correct? Article 262 deals with adjudication of inter-state river water disputes and bars Supreme Court jurisdiction in such matters — R is factually correct.

Step 3 — Does R explain A? The Union's authority to legislate on interlinking derives from Entry 56, not from Article 262. Article 262 governs dispute resolution machinery — it does not grant legislative competence for interlinking. R does not explain A.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This trap exploits the proximity of Entry 56 and Article 262 in the constitutional scheme. Both relate to inter-state rivers, so students who know both facts tend to assume they are causally connected. However, Entry 56 provides the legislative competence for river development, while Article 262 provides the dispute resolution mechanism — they serve different constitutional functions. A student with superficial recall will select (a); only precise constitutional knowledge reveals they are independent provisions.
solution.final_explanation:
India's constitutional framework for inter-state rivers has two distinct pillars that are frequently confused in examination settings.

Assertion (A) — Correct: Entry 56 of the Union List empowers Parliament to legislate on the regulation and development of inter-state rivers and river valleys if declared by Parliament to be expedient in the public interest. This is the primary constitutional basis for Union involvement in river interlinking.

Reason (R) — Correct: Article 262 provides a mechanism for adjudication of inter-state water disputes and explicitly bars the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court or any other court in such disputes — enabling tribunal-based resolution.

Causal link — Does NOT hold: The Union's authority to pursue river interlinking flows from Entry 56, not from Article 262. Article 262 operates in the dispute resolution domain, not the domain of affirmative legislative competence for development. They are independent constitutional provisions serving different purposes.

Value Addition:
• Entry 17 (State List) covers water storage and irrigation as state subjects — the Union's authority under Entry 56 is specifically limited to inter-state rivers.
• The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 was enacted under Article 262.
• The Supreme Court's 2012 directive on NRLP came through PIL jurisdiction, not under Article 262.

solution.concept_anchor: NRLP origin — chronological sequence of proposals
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who recall that NWDA was established 'around the 1980s' and that the Supreme Court was involved 'recently' may correctly order those two but swap K.L. Rao and Dastur, choosing (b).
elimination_logic: K.L. Rao proposed the Ganga-Cauvery link in 1972 — this is the earliest anchor event.
Captain Dastur's Garland Canal concept was also from the early 1970s but is generally placed after Rao's proposal in the institutional record — comes second.
NWDA was established in 1982 — third in sequence.
The Supreme Court's directive mandating time-bound implementation and a Special Committee came in 2012 — the most recent; correct order is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap lies between K.L. Rao and Captain Dastur — both proposed their concepts in the early 1970s, and many students are uncertain which came first. Additionally, students who memorise NWDA as '1980s' without knowing the precise year may misplace it relative to Dastur. The 2012 Supreme Court directive is typically known but students may confuse whether it preceded or followed the MoU for Ken-Betwa (2005).
solution.final_explanation:
The evolution of India's river interlinking concept passed through distinct phases from individual visionary proposals to institutional frameworks and judicial directives.

Correct sequence:
1. K.L. Rao's Ganga-Cauvery link proposal (1972) — the seminal technical concept.
2. Captain Dastur's Garland Canal proposal (early 1970s, after Rao) — an alternative conceptual framework involving a network of canals around peninsular India.
3. Establishment of NWDA (1982) — formal institutional response to these proposals.
4. Supreme Court's directive mandating time-bound implementation (2012) — judicial push for action.

Option (c) correctly places these in sequence: Rao → Dastur → NWDA → Supreme Court directive.

Value Addition:
• Dastur's Garland Canal was considered more ambitious and less technically feasible than Rao's targeted link.
• The 2012 Supreme Court order arose from a PIL filed by Suresh Prabhakar Prabhu.
• The Special Committee formed after the 2012 directive was chaired by a former Chief Justice of India.

solution.concept_anchor: Interlinking and existing tribunal awards — not bypassed
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Article 262 governs inter-state water disputes may assume it directly applies here, missing that the scenario involves planning-stage interlinking where Entry 56 is more directly operative.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a situation where an approved interlinking project involves diverting water from a river whose allocation is already fixed by a tribunal — this tests whether interlinking overrides tribunal awards.
Eliminate (a): The Union cannot unilaterally override a tribunal award; state consent and fresh agreements are required.

Eliminate (b): While Article 262 governs dispute adjudication, it does not by itself permit the Union to proceed without state consent — the scenario is about a planning conflict, not a dispute adjudication.
Eliminate (c): No constitutional provision permits automatic override of tribunal awards through an interlinking project approval.

Confirm (d): Interlinking does not bypass existing tribunal awards — it requires fresh agreements among basin states, as the interlinking framework operates alongside, not above, existing water-sharing arrangements.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap of 'scope extension' operates here: students may assume that a Cabinet-approved interlinking project carries sufficient authority to supersede existing tribunal awards. This is incorrect — interlinking projects must work within the framework of existing awards, and fresh interstate agreements are necessary. The scenario is designed to test whether candidates know that NRLP implementation is legally subordinate to tribunal-determined state entitlements.
solution.final_explanation:
A fundamental but frequently misunderstood aspect of India's river interlinking framework is its relationship with existing inter-state water tribunal awards.

The applicable principle: Interlinking projects do NOT automatically override or bypass the allocations made by inter-state water dispute tribunals. Even after Cabinet approval, an interlinking project that involves a river with an existing tribunal award requires fresh inter-state agreements. The Union cannot unilaterally proceed against established state entitlements.

Applied to the scenario: The downstream state's objection is legally valid. The tribunal award continues to bind water-sharing arrangements. Proceeding with the diversion without the downstream state's consent would violate the tribunal's allocation.

• Option (a): Incorrect — Cabinet approval does not override state water rights established by tribunal.
• Option (b): Incorrect — Article 262 provides the dispute resolution forum, not a bypass mechanism.
• Option (c): Incorrect — there is no automatic override provision in the constitutional scheme for interlinking.
• Option (d): Correct — fresh agreements among basin states are mandatory.

Value Addition:
• Tamil Nadu's opposition to certain interlinking proposals is rooted in exactly this concern regarding Cauvery water entitlements.
• Odisha has similarly objected to Mahanadi diversions without fresh agreements.
• The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 tribunal awards have the force of an order of the Supreme Court.

solution.concept_anchor: Brahmaputra surplus basin — not deficit
solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who associate Rajasthan with water scarcity and know it is a 'deficit' region may doubt whether it belongs with Mahanadi and Godavari, potentially selecting (d) instead of (a).
elimination_logic: The question asks which does NOT belong among water-surplus river basins as identified for NRLP.
Mahanadi, Godavari, and Brahmaputra are all identified as surplus basins in NWDA's framework — they are donors in the interlinking concept.
The Luni river basin (Rajasthan) is a seasonal, largely arid basin identified as deficit — it does NOT belong among surplus basins.
The odd one out is (a): Luni.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The UPSC trap here targets students who assume 'all southern rivers are deficit' (a common misconception addressed in the Peninsular component key dimensions). Mahanadi and Godavari are clearly surplus. Brahmaputra is the largest surplus basin. A partially prepared student might question Brahmaputra's classification — particularly given that its waters remain largely unharnessed — and miss that Luni is the obvious odd one out as a deficit/arid basin.
solution.final_explanation:
NWDA's surplus-deficit framework is central to understanding which basins donate water and which receive it under NRLP.

• Option (a) — Luni: This is the odd one out. The Luni is a seasonal river of arid Rajasthan, draining into the Rann of Kutch. It is a water-deficit basin, not a surplus donor.
• Option (b) — Mahanadi: Identified as a surplus basin; the Mahanadi is the starting point of the Peninsular cascade (Mahanadi → Godavari → Krishna → Cauvery).
• Option (c) — Brahmaputra: The largest surplus basin in India by volume — yet largely unharnessed due to geopolitics, terrain, and ecology.
• Option (d) — Godavari: India's second-largest river by discharge; clearly identified as surplus and a key cascade node.

Value Addition:
• NWDA uses a 75% dependability criterion to assess surplus water availability.
• Not all southern rivers are deficit: Mahanadi, Godavari have surplus; Cauvery is deficit.
• Brahmaputra's surplus remains largely theoretical for interlinking due to Chinese upstream projects and terrain.

statement_analysis.statement: The National Water Policy, 2012 supports river interlinking while placing drinking water above irrigation in the priority hierarchy for water use.
statement_analysis.reason: NWP 2012 endorses interlinking as part of integrated water resources management and explicitly prioritises drinking water over irrigation, hydropower, and navigation.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know NWP 2012 is an important and detailed document may assume it has statutory standing, selecting (a) believing both statements are correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: NWP 2012's priority hierarchy (drinking > irrigation > hydropower > navigation) is well-established; its support for interlinking is explicit — Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: NWP 2012 is a policy resolution, not an Act of Parliament — it has no statutory force. The River Boards Act exists separately and is not the enforcement mechanism for NWP — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the common assumption that a document as comprehensive and authoritative as the NWP must have statutory force. In reality, NWP 2012 is a Cabinet-approved policy resolution — it guides but does not legally bind. The mention of the River Boards Act, 1956 as an enforcement mechanism adds plausibility because that Act does exist and relates to river development, but it does not enforce NWP provisions. This is a classic scope-extension trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The National Water Policy (2012) is India's framework document for integrated water resources management but its legal status is often misunderstood.

• Statement 1 — Correct: NWP 2012 supports interlinking within an integrated framework and establishes the use hierarchy: drinking water first, then irrigation, followed by hydropower, navigation, and other uses.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: NWP 2012 is a policy document — it carries no statutory force and cannot be enforced through courts. The River Boards Act, 1956 is an independent law enabling the central government to establish river boards for specified inter-state rivers; it does not serve as the enforcement arm of the NWP.

Value Addition:
• Draft NWP 2020 shifts emphasis toward demand-side management and groundwater recharge over large infrastructure projects.
• River Boards Act, 1956 has never actually been invoked to constitute a river board for any river in India.
• Jal Shakti Abhiyan and Atal Bhujal Yojana are more recent complementary initiatives for water conservation.

solution.concept_anchor: NWDA legal status — registered society not statutory body
solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Statutory authority under an Act of Parliament' sounds authoritative and is the form most government technical bodies take, making it a compelling wrong choice.
elimination_logic: NWDA was not established by an Act of Parliament — eliminate option (c) which claims statutory authority.
NWDA is not a constitutional body — eliminate option (d).
NWDA cannot implement projects; it only prepares feasibility reports and DPRs — eliminate option (a) which claims implementation authority.
NWDA was established as a registered society under the Societies Registration Act — confirm option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students familiar with bodies like the Central Water Commission (a statutory body) or NHPC (a PSU) tend to assume NWDA has similar statutory standing. The plausible-fabrication trap presents 'statutory authority' as an option that sounds exactly right for a government technical agency of this scale. In reality, NWDA's status as a registered society is a critically important legal nuance — it explains why NWDA has no power to enforce agreements or adjudicate disputes.
solution.final_explanation:
The National Water Development Agency (NWDA) occupies a unique institutional position in India's water governance architecture.

• Option (a): Incorrect — NWDA does not implement projects. Implementation responsibility lies with state governments and designated project authorities.
• Option (b): Correct — NWDA was established in 1982 as a registered society under the Societies Registration Act, under the Ministry of Water Resources (now Jal Shakti). This means it is not a statutory body and cannot enforce agreements.
• Option (c): Incorrect — NWDA has no statutory basis in an Act of Parliament; it is a society, not a statutory authority.
• Option (d): Incorrect — NWDA is not a constitutional body; it derives no authority from the Constitution directly.

Value Addition:
• Compare: Central Water Commission is a statutory body; NWDA is a registered society — an important distinction.
• NWDA's core mandate: surveys, investigations, preparation of feasibility/DPR reports for interlinking links.
• NWDA has no dispute-resolution powers — purely a technical body.

solution.concept_anchor: Environmental impacts — Panna Tiger Reserve and Ken-Betwa
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who associate Chilika Lake with conservation concerns and know Mahanadi diversion is being discussed may accept option (c) as a settled fact, when in fact Chilika's potential impact from Mahanadi diversion is still a projected concern, not an established submergence.
elimination_logic: Option (a): Daudhan Dam on Ken-Betwa is specifically proposed within Panna Tiger Reserve — this is the most precisely documented environmental conflict in NRLP — this pair is correctly matched.

Option (b): Hilsa is a migratory fish species that is affected by longitudinal river connectivity disruption, not specifically by the Ken-Betwa link — the pairing of Ken-Betwa with Hilsa is an entity-swap.
Option (c): Chilika Lake's ecology is a concern related to potential Mahanadi diversion, but Chilika itself is not a 'submergence' from interlinking — the pairing is imprecise.
Option (d): The Farakka Barrage is associated with the Ganga, not with any direct interlinking project submergence — this is a conflation of distinct interventions.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in Option (b) associates Hilsa fish with Ken-Betwa specifically, when Hilsa's concern is broader — related to longitudinal connectivity disruption across multiple river systems, particularly the Ganga-Brahmaputra corridor. Students who know both facts (Ken-Betwa and Hilsa concerns in interlinking) may incorrectly validate this pairing.
solution.final_explanation:
Environmental impact assessment is a critical dimension of river interlinking that the Supreme Court's 2012 order mandated for each link separately.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: The Daudhan Dam, the primary storage structure for the Ken-Betwa link, is proposed inside Panna Tiger Reserve in Madhya Pradesh. This is the most documented biodiversity conflict within NRLP.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: While Hilsa is indeed vulnerable to river connectivity disruption from interlinking, it is not specifically linked to the Ken-Betwa project (which is in the Yamuna-Vindhyan basin, far from Hilsa habitat).
• Option (c) — Imprecisely matched: Chilika Lake's ecology may be affected by reduced Mahanadi flows, but it faces no direct submergence from interlinking.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: Farakka Barrage is a flow modification structure on the Ganga, not an interlinking submergence case.

Value Addition:
• Panna Tiger Reserve hosted India's first tiger reintroduction (2009) after local extinction.
• Hilsa and Mahseer are the two migratory fish species most cited in interlinking environmental assessments.
• EIA is mandatory for each link project separately under the 2012 Supreme Court directive.

solution.concept_anchor: Bangladesh 1996 Ganga Treaty and transboundary interlinking concerns

statement_analysis.statement: Nepal's territory would be required for the construction of storage reservoirs proposed under the Himalayan component of NRLP, making Nepalese cooperation indispensable.
statement_analysis.reason: Major storage structures on Kosi, Gandak, and Ghaghra tributaries are proposed in Nepali territory, requiring bilateral treaty arrangements.

statement_analysis.statement: The 1996 Ganga Water Treaty between India and Bangladesh covers the sharing of Brahmaputra waters at Farakka.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1996 Ganga Water Treaty (Farakka Treaty) covers the sharing of Ganga waters at Farakka — not Brahmaputra waters. Bangladesh's concern about Brahmaputra diversion is separate from this treaty.

statement_analysis.statement: China's upstream dam projects on the Brahmaputra complicate India's surplus water calculations for the Himalayan interlinking component.
statement_analysis.reason: Projects like Zangmu and Motuo on the upper Brahmaputra (in Tibet) could potentially alter downstream flow volumes, affecting the reliability of India's surplus estimates for the Brahmaputra basin.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know the 1996 Ganga Treaty is 'about Farakka and sharing of river water with Bangladesh' may incorrectly validate Statement 2 without checking which river is covered, selecting option (d).
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Nepal's territory is essential for Himalayan reservoir sites — Statement 1 is correct.
Examine Statement 2 carefully: The 1996 treaty is the Ganga Water Treaty covering Ganga flows at Farakka — it does NOT cover Brahmaputra — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: China's Zangmu and Motuo projects on the Tsangpo-Brahmaputra are well-documented geopolitical complicating factors — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a classic partial-truth trap: every element in it is almost right. The 1996 treaty is real, Bangladesh is involved, and it is about water sharing. But the treaty covers the Ganga at Farakka, not the Brahmaputra. Students who recall the treaty without recalling its specific river coverage will accept Statement 2 as correct and choose option (d) instead of (c).
solution.final_explanation:
River interlinking's geopolitical dimensions extend beyond India's borders, involving Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, and indirectly China.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Himalayan component's viability is critically dependent on Nepal's cooperation for constructing storage reservoirs on the Kosi, Gandak, and Ghaghra systems — rivers that flow from Nepal into Bihar.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Ganga Water Treaty of 1996 (also called the Farakka Treaty) governs sharing of Ganga waters between India and Bangladesh at Farakka. It does not cover the Brahmaputra. Bangladesh's concerns about interlinking relate to potential reductions in lean-season flows in both rivers.
• Statement 3 — Correct: China's Zangmu dam (operational since 2015) and the proposed Motuo mega-dam on the Brahmaputra raise serious concerns about upstream regulation that would alter the flow volumes on which India's surplus calculations are based.

Value Addition:
• The 1996 Ganga Treaty is a 30-year agreement for the sharing of Ganga flows at Farakka.
• Bhutan is a partner for storage on eastern Himalayan tributaries like the Sankosh.
• Bangladesh depends on the Brahmaputra and Ganga for agriculture, navigation, and ecology in its delta region.

solution.concept_anchor: 75% dependability criterion — NWDA surplus assessment
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who associate 'surplus' with maximum possible water availability may select option (a), assuming NWDA uses peak flow data, which would overestimate usable surplus.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Using average annual flow would overestimate reliable surplus by including wet years — NWDA uses a dependability criterion, not average flow.
Eliminate (c): A 90% dependability criterion is used for drinking water reliability assessments — not for NWDA's surplus basin methodology.
Eliminate (d): Monsoon peak discharge data would massively overstate surplus — seasonal and year-specific variation is specifically a critique of static surplus models.
Confirm (b): NWDA uses a 75% dependability criterion — meaning water availability is assured in 75 out of 100 years — as the standard for identifying surplus basins.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap here adds 'peak discharge' or 'average annual flow' as alternatives that sound plausible for measuring basin surplus. Students who have not specifically studied the 75% dependability criterion may assume average flow is the logical basis. The 90% figure in option (c) is a plausible distractor because it is used in other water resource contexts, particularly drinking water reliability standards.
solution.final_explanation:
NWDA's methodology for identifying surplus and deficit basins is a technical dimension that appears in advanced UPSC questions on NRLP.

• Option (a): Incorrect — average annual flow includes both wet and dry years, overstating reliable surplus. NWDA uses a dependability-based criterion.
• Option (b): Correct — the 75% dependability criterion means water availability at the assessed quantity is guaranteed in 75 out of every 100 years. Basins with water availability exceeding their utilisable demand at this dependability level are classified as surplus.
• Option (c): Incorrect — 90% dependability is a stricter standard used for drinking water supply projects; it is not NWDA's criterion for surplus basin identification.
• Option (d): Incorrect — monsoon peak discharge figures would grossly overestimate year-round surplus and are not used for this purpose.

Value Addition:
• A key critique: surplus/deficit designations change between monsoon and lean seasons — the static 75% model does not capture this dynamic.
• 'Utilisable water resources' (considering storage, extraction feasibility) differs from 'water availability' (total flow) — another NWDA methodology trap.
• Climate change is making historical flow data less reliable as a basis for these calculations.

solution.concept_anchor: Ken-Betwa displacement — FRA 2006 and LARR 2013 applicability

statement_analysis.statement: Land acquisition for the Ken-Betwa Link Project is governed by the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.
statement_analysis.reason: The LARR Act 2013 applies to all government land acquisition in India including for interlinking projects — this statement is correct and therefore not an answer to a 'NOT correct' question.

statement_analysis.statement: The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 has no applicability to forest land submergence under the Daudhan Dam, as interlinking is a national security project.
statement_analysis.reason: The Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006 applies to all forest land diversion including for dam construction — there is no 'national security' exemption from FRA for interlinking projects.

statement_analysis.statement: Displacement from the Ken-Betwa project primarily affects tribal and agrarian communities of the Bundelkhand region.
statement_analysis.reason: Panna district (Daudhan Dam area) has significant Scheduled Tribe and agrarian populations — approximately 10,000 families are estimated to be displaced.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know LARR 2013 applies to all projects may wrongly flag Statement 1 as potentially inapplicable to 'special' national projects, choosing (a).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: LARR 2013 applies to all government land acquisition — there is no exemption for interlinking; Statement 1 is correct, not an incorrect statement.
Evaluate Statement 2: FRA 2006 applies to forest land diversion regardless of the project type; no 'national security' exemption exists for interlinking — Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Bundelkhand's tribal and agrarian communities facing displacement is well-documented — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 deploys a fabricated 'national security exemption' for FRA 2006. Students who know that some emergency situations allow procedural relaxations (like defence projects getting expedited clearances) may extend this incorrectly to interlinking projects. The Forest Rights Act has no such blanket exemption, and forest diversion for dam projects requires explicit gram sabha consent under FRA. The temporal-swap distractor lies in suggesting the older pre-2006 framework governs when FRA 2006 clearly applies.
solution.final_explanation:
Social and legal dimensions of displacement from interlinking projects involve overlapping frameworks that must be understood precisely.

• Statement 1 — Correct: LARR 2013 governs land acquisition for Ken-Betwa and mandates fair compensation, rehabilitation, and resettlement — no exemption exists for interlinking projects.
• Statement 2 — NOT Correct: The Forest Rights Act, 2006 fully applies to forest land diversion for the Daudhan Dam. There is no 'national security' exemption from FRA for river interlinking. FRA requires gram sabha consent before forest diversion, which has been a major procedural hurdle.
• Statement 3 — Correct: An estimated 10,000 families, largely tribal and agrarian, face displacement from the Daudhan submergence zone in Bundelkhand.

Value Addition:
• FRA 2006 gram sabha consent is mandatory for forest diversion — it cannot be bypassed for developmental projects.
• The Sardar Sarovar Project displacement is the standard historical reference for large dam social impact assessments in India.
• Bundelkhand is one of India's most water-stressed and poverty-concentrated regions — creating both urgency for the project and vulnerability for displaced communities.

solution.concept_anchor: Watershed management success stories and MGNREGS linkage

statement_analysis.statement: Ralegan Siddhi (Maharashtra) is a widely cited success story of community-led watershed development that transformed a water-deficit village.
statement_analysis.reason: Ralegan Siddhi in Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra, is the watershed management model associated with Anna Hazare — a landmark case of decentralised water conservation.

statement_analysis.statement: Hiware Bazar (Maharashtra) is another watershed development success, often cited alongside Ralegan Siddhi as demonstrating in-situ water conservation at village scale.
statement_analysis.reason: Hiware Bazar in Ahmednagar district achieved groundwater recharge and agricultural transformation through watershed development and is a documented model village.

statement_analysis.statement: Watershed development activities under MGNREGS are administered by the Ministry of Jal Shakti as the sole nodal ministry.
statement_analysis.reason: Natural resource management including watershed activities under MGNREGS is administered by the Ministry of Rural Development — not the Ministry of Jal Shakti.

statement_analysis.statement: The watershed management approach is fundamentally decentralised and in-situ — contrasting with interlinking's large-scale inter-basin water transfer model.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the core conceptual distinction: watershed management conserves water at the source through local soil-water conservation, while interlinking transfers water across basins through large infrastructure.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who associate Jal Shakti with all water-related programmes may accept Statement 3 as correct, choosing 'All four' as the answer.
elimination_logic: Validate pair 1: Ralegan Siddhi is the canonical watershed success story — correct.
Validate pair 2: Hiware Bazar is a well-known companion case from the same district — correct.
Check pair 3: MGNREGS is under the Ministry of Rural Development, not Jal Shakti — incorrect.
Validate pair 4: The decentralised vs. centralised contrast is the core paradigm difference — correct.
Three pairs are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap in Statement 3 places Jal Shakti in the role of MGNREGS nodal ministry. Since Jal Shakti administers water-related programmes including Atal Bhujal Yojana and Jal Shakti Abhiyan, students who associate watershed activities with water management incorrectly assign administrative control to Jal Shakti rather than Rural Development.
solution.final_explanation:
The watershed management vs. large interlinking infrastructure debate is a key paradigmatic tension in India's water policy discourse.

• Pair 1 — Correct: Ralegan Siddhi (Anna Hazare's village) in Ahmednagar district is a landmark of community watershed development.
• Pair 2 — Correct: Hiware Bazar, also in Ahmednagar, achieved near-complete village transformation through participatory watershed management.
• Pair 3 — Incorrect: MGNREGS, including its natural resource management and watershed component, is administered by the Ministry of Rural Development — not the Ministry of Jal Shakti. This is a common institutional confusion in examinations.
• Pair 4 — Correct: Watershed management's defining characteristic is in-situ, decentralised conservation — as opposed to interlinking's inter-basin transfers requiring massive infrastructure.

Value Addition:
• NITI Aayog supports both approaches but has increasingly emphasised demand-side management.
• Jal Shakti Abhiyan (2019) and Atal Bhujal Yojana are under Jal Shakti — distinct from MGNREGS watershed works.
• Ralegan Siddhi and Hiware Bazar are in the drought-prone Ahmednagar district of Maharashtra.

solution.concept_anchor: IWAI — navigation governed separately from interlinking
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both facts are true (NW Act 2016 declared 111 waterways, and interlinking canals have navigation potential) may assume they are causally connected and choose (a).
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? The National Waterways Act, 2016 declared 111 national waterways and several proposed interlinked corridors do overlap with these waterways — A is factually correct.

Step 2 — Is R correct? The Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI) operates under the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, which is a separate ministry from Jal Shakti (which governs interlinking) — R is factually correct.

Step 3 — Does R explain A? The separate governance of waterways development by IWAI explains why navigation is only a tertiary benefit of interlinking, not its driver — but R explains why they remain institutionally separate, not why the 2016 Act was passed. The causal link between these two independent facts is weak — R does not causally explain the 111-waterway declaration in A.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT causally explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges two related but institutionally separate domains: NRLP (under Jal Shakti) and national waterways development (under IWAI/Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways). Students who know both facts tend to link them causally — the 111 waterways seem to follow from interlinking plans, and IWAI's separate mandate seems to explain the interlinking framework. In reality, the National Waterways Act 2016 and NRLP are independent policy tracks that happen to overlap geographically in some corridors.
solution.final_explanation:
Navigation is frequently cited as a tertiary benefit of river interlinking, but its governance sits in an entirely different institutional framework.

Assertion (A) — Correct: The National Waterways Act, 2016 declared 111 national waterways, and several of these overlap geographically with corridors proposed under the interlinking programme.

Reason (R) — Correct: IWAI operates under the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways — a ministry separate from the Ministry of Jal Shakti that governs NRLP and NWDA.

Causal link — Does NOT hold: R explains the institutional separation between the two programmes but does not causally explain the 111-waterway declaration in A. The National Waterways Act 2016 was passed for independent navigational and economic reasons, not as a consequence of NRLP. The two are parallel policy tracks, not cause and effect.

Value Addition:
• Jal Marg Vikas Project (NW-1: Ganga, Allahabad to Haldia) is IWAI's flagship navigation project.
• Navigation is listed as a co-benefit of NRLP but is NOT its design objective.
• The Ganga-Cauvery axis, if ever interlinked, would theoretically create India's longest navigable corridor.

solution.concept_anchor: Farakka Barrage — unintended consequences precedent
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Farakka is associated with Bangladesh and sedimentation problems may attribute sedimentation issues to the Ganga delta, not to the Kolkata Port — making option (c) seem plausible.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): Farakka is on the Ganga in West Bengal, not on the Brahmaputra — a geographic-swap distractor.
Eliminate (c): While sedimentation is a Farakka issue, the primary stated purpose was improving navigability for Kolkata Port, not reducing downstream erosion.
Eliminate (d): Farakka Barrage is in West Bengal, India — not in Bangladesh.

Confirm (a): Farakka Barrage was constructed to increase water flow into the Hooghly river to maintain navigability of Kolkata Port — and it is cited as a precedent for unintended consequences of river flow modification.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap places Farakka on the Brahmaputra (option b) — a plausible error for students who associate both Farakka and Brahmaputra with Bangladesh's water concerns. The correct association is Farakka with the Ganga in West Bengal. The Farakka experience (reduced flows into Bangladesh during lean season, unexpected sedimentation patterns, fishery impacts) is invoked as a cautionary precedent in NRLP discussions.
solution.final_explanation:
The Farakka Barrage is repeatedly invoked in river interlinking debates as a cautionary example of unintended consequences from river flow modification.

• Option (a) — Correct: Farakka Barrage was built to divert Ganga waters into the Hooghly river to flush out sedimentation and restore navigability for Kolkata Port. Its construction had unintended consequences including altered sedimentation patterns and reduced dry-season flows into Bangladesh.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Farakka is on the Ganga in Murshidabad district, West Bengal — not on the Brahmaputra.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Reducing downstream river bank erosion was not the stated primary purpose — improving Kolkata Port navigability was.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Farakka Barrage is located in India (West Bengal), not in Bangladesh.

Value Addition:
• The 1996 Ganga Water Treaty (India-Bangladesh) was negotiated largely because of Farakka-related flow reduction into Bangladesh.
• Farakka's unintended consequences include increased flooding in Bihar and altered fishery patterns.
• In NRLP debates, Farakka is cited to argue that flow modifications have complex, non-linear downstream effects.

solution.concept_anchor: Climate change and NRLP surplus-deficit projections

statement_analysis.statement: NRLP's foundational surplus-deficit calculations are based on historical river flow data, making them potentially unreliable as climate change alters monsoon patterns.
statement_analysis.reason: NWDA's surplus/deficit designation methodology relies on historical flow records; climate-induced monsoon variability undermines the assumption that historical patterns will persist.

statement_analysis.reason: Flash floods are rapid, localised events that interlinking infrastructure cannot intercept or manage effectively; interlinking addresses seasonal surplus diversion, not flash flood peaks.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who accept that glacial retreat affects Himalayan rivers (Statement 2 correct) but doubt the flash flood claim (Statement 3) may incorrectly decide Statement 3 is also correct, choosing (b) thinking all three are correct — but option (b) is '2 and 3 only'.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: NRLP uses historical data; climate change altering monsoon patterns is a documented critique — correct.
Statement 2: Glacial retreat reducing lean-season baseflow in glacially-fed Himalayan rivers is a well-established climate impact concern — correct.
Statement 3: Flash floods are sudden, high-intensity events; interlinking is designed for seasonal surplus management and cannot effectively address flash flooding — incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a scope-extension trap: interlinking does help manage seasonal surplus flows and to some extent reduce flood peaks from sustained heavy rainfall over weeks. Students may extend this to include flash floods — which are qualitatively different events occurring over hours, not seasons. The interlinking system cannot fill and release reservoirs fast enough to manage flash flood events; different interventions (early warning systems, floodplain zoning) are needed for those.
solution.final_explanation:
Climate change introduces a layer of uncertainty that fundamentally challenges NRLP's foundational assumptions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: NWDA's entire surplus-deficit framework is built on historical river discharge data. If climate change shifts monsoon patterns — making some historically surplus seasons deficit and vice versa — the identification of donor and recipient basins becomes unreliable.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Himalayan component depends on perennial river flows partly sustained by glacial meltwater. As Himalayan glaciers retreat, dry-season baseflows will decline, eroding the very surplus the component is designed to harness.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Flash floods are sudden, localised precipitation events. Interlinking infrastructure is designed to move seasonal water surpluses over weeks and months — it cannot respond to flash flood timescales. Effective flash flood management requires different tools: early warning systems, floodplain zoning, and upstream catchment management.

Value Addition:
• Dynamic water accounting frameworks (instead of static historical models) are recommended for climate-resilient water planning.
• Extended droughts and increased flood frequency — both products of climate change — create contradictory demands that interlinking can only partially address.
• IPCC reports identify the Hindu Kush-Himalayan glaciers as among the fastest retreating globally.

solution.final_explanation:
Western India's interlinking proposals involve two distinct links targeting different deficit regions.

solution.concept_anchor: Andhra Pradesh bifurcation and Godavari-Krishna interstate dynamics
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Polavaram is declared a National Project may assume that Central Government control resolves state-level water-sharing disputes automatically, selecting (c).
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a state formed after Andhra Pradesh's bifurcation (2014) contesting water allocations under a pre-bifurcation framework — this tests knowledge of how state reorganisation affects inter-state water arrangements.
Eliminate (a): Polavaram's National Project status relates to funding, not water-sharing authority — it does not resolve interstate allocation disputes.
Eliminate (c): National Project status does not transfer water allocation adjudication to the Union — inter-state water disputes still go to tribunals.
Eliminate (d): There is no automatic 50-50 split provision when a state bifurcates — allocations must be renegotiated or adjudicated.

Confirm (b): Andhra Pradesh's bifurcation in 2014 created new interstate dynamics requiring fresh water-sharing arrangements between Telangana and residual Andhra Pradesh for rivers including Godavari and Krishna — the correct applicable principle.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) is the strong partial-truth distractor: Polavaram IS a National Project (declared under the AP Reorganisation Act 2014), and the Central Government does have enhanced authority over it. However, National Project status is about financing and construction oversight — it does not grant the Centre authority to unilaterally allocate water shares between successor states. The correct principle is that state bifurcation requires fresh water-sharing frameworks, often necessitating new tribunal proceedings.
solution.final_explanation:
The Andhra Pradesh bifurcation of 2014 created one of India's most complex post-reorganisation water governance challenges, with direct implications for the Peninsular interlinking cascade.

Applicable principle: When a state reorganisation bifurcates a river basin state, the successor states must renegotiate or seek fresh adjudication of water-sharing arrangements. Pre-bifurcation allocations do not automatically continue for successor states in altered proportions.

• Option (a): Incorrect — Polavaram's National Project status addresses construction financing, not water allocation authority.
• Option (b): Correct — The 2014 bifurcation created new interstate riparian relationships between Telangana and Andhra Pradesh for Godavari and Krishna waters, requiring fresh arrangements independent of pre-bifurcation agreements.
• Option (c): Incorrect — National Project designation does not transfer water allocation adjudication to the Centre; tribunals remain the correct forum.
• Option (d): Incorrect — No automatic 50-50 or proportional split applies upon bifurcation; population and agricultural area ratios are argued but must be adjudicated.

Value Addition:
• The AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 declared Polavaram a National Project and mandated the Central Government to complete it.
• A new Krishna River Management Board and Godavari River Management Board were created post-bifurcation.
• This scenario directly affects the Mahanadi-Godavari-Krishna-Cauvery cascade's feasibility.

solution.concept_anchor: Atal Bhujal Yojana — groundwater scheme vs. interlinking
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who associate the Indira Gandhi Canal with Rajasthan waterlogging problems may question whether it belongs with 'groundwater recharge' examples rather than the 'cautionary examples' of interlinking.
elimination_logic: The question asks which does NOT relate to the theme of canal seepage contributing to groundwater recharge or waterlogging from irrigation infrastructure.
Indira Gandhi Canal (Rajasthan) — canal seepage causing waterlogging is the cautionary example from this canal: related.
Punjab-Haryana high water table — canal irrigation-induced waterlogging: related.

Atal Bhujal Yojana — a direct groundwater augmentation and management scheme focused on community-level groundwater governance: this is an alternative approach, not a canal seepage/waterlogging example.
Jal Shakti Abhiyan — water conservation mission with groundwater recharge as a goal: related to groundwater but operates at mission/campaign level.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap here merges Atal Bhujal Yojana (a direct groundwater governance programme) with canal-seepage-based recharge examples. Students who know Atal Bhujal Yojana relates to groundwater may incorrectly group it with the canal-seepage/waterlogging cluster. The distinction is that Atal Bhujal Yojana is a World Bank-funded community-based groundwater management programme — not a canal or surface water infrastructure example.
solution.final_explanation:
Groundwater recharge and waterlogging risks from canal-based irrigation systems are the indirect hydrological consequences of large surface water projects.

• Option (a) — Atal Bhujal Yojana: This is the odd one out. It is a Central Sector Scheme for groundwater management in water-stressed areas, implemented with World Bank support. It is not a canal irrigation or surface water transfer project — it focuses on demand-side groundwater governance and recharge at community level.
• Option (b) — Indira Gandhi Canal: Canal seepage from the Rajasthan Canal system has caused waterlogging and salinization in parts of Rajasthan — a direct cautionary example for interlinking projects.
• Option (c) — Punjab-Haryana experience: Decades of canal irrigation have raised water tables in parts of Punjab and Haryana, causing waterlogging — another cautionary case.
• Option (d) — Jal Shakti Abhiyan: A mission for water conservation including groundwater recharge, linked to water security initiatives.

Value Addition:
• Atal Bhujal Yojana covers seven states: Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, MP, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, UP.
• The difference between recharge (beneficial) and waterlogging (harmful) depends on the depth of the water table.
• Salinization, not just waterlogging, is the long-term threat in arid canal command areas.

solution.concept_anchor: Entry 56 vs Article 262 — distinct constitutional provisions

statement_analysis.statement: Entry 17 of the State List confers exclusive authority on states over water storage and irrigation, completely preventing any Union intervention in river interlinking.
statement_analysis.reason: While Entry 17 places water storage and irrigation with states, Entry 56 of the Union List gives Parliament authority over inter-state rivers in public interest — this overrides the exclusivity implied in the statement.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court's 2012 directive on river networking arose from a Public Interest Litigation and directed formation of a high-powered committee for time-bound implementation.
statement_analysis.reason: The PIL was filed by Suresh Prabhakar Prabhu; the Supreme Court directed formation of a Special Committee and mandated time-bound action — this is factually accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: River interlinking has a dedicated constitutional provision analogous to Article 262 for interstate water disputes, which provides a specific legal pathway for inter-basin water transfers.
statement_analysis.reason: There is no dedicated constitutional provision for river interlinking — it relies on Parliament's legislative competence under Entry 56 of the Union List; Article 262 specifically governs dispute adjudication, not inter-basin transfers.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who recall that the 2012 Supreme Court directive existed may doubt Statement 2's specifics (the PIL filer's name) and incorrectly flag it as 'NOT correct', choosing option (b).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Entry 17 gives states authority over water, BUT Entry 56 gives Parliament overriding authority for inter-state rivers — the claim of 'complete prevention' of Union intervention is false; Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: The PIL by Suresh Prabhakar Prabhu and the Supreme Court's 2012 directive with a high-powered committee is documented — Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: No dedicated constitutional provision exists for interlinking; it relies on Entry 56 — the analogy with Article 262 is fabricated; Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses a scope-extension technique: Entry 17 does give states primary authority over water, but adding 'completely preventing any Union intervention' overstates its scope, because Entry 56 creates a clear carve-out for inter-state rivers. Statement 3 fabricates a constitutional provision analogous to Article 262 for interlinking — an appealing distractor because Article 262 is closely associated with river water management.
solution.final_explanation:
India's constitutional framework for rivers involves a delicate balance between state subject (Entry 17) and Union authority (Entry 56).

• Statement 1 — NOT Correct: Entry 17 (State List) covers water for intrastate purposes, but Entry 56 (Union List) explicitly empowers Parliament to regulate and develop inter-state rivers 'in public interest' — so Union intervention through interlinking legislation is constitutionally valid.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 2012 Supreme Court directive in the Networking of Rivers case (PIL by Suresh Prabhakar Prabhu) ordered the formation of a Special Committee chaired by a former Chief Justice and directed time-bound implementation.
• Statement 3 — NOT Correct: River interlinking has no dedicated constitutional provision. Unlike inter-state water disputes (Article 262), interlinking relies solely on Parliament's legislative competence under Entry 56. There is no Article analogous to 262 for inter-basin transfers.

Value Addition:
• Entry 56 requires Parliament to declare by law that such regulation is expedient in the public interest.
• The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 operationalises Article 262 for dispute resolution.
• NRLP implementation does not require a constitutional amendment — it operates under existing Entry 56 competence.

solution.concept_anchor: Not all southern rivers are deficit — NWDA methodology trap
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who have a general impression that peninsular rivers are 'smaller' and therefore deficit may accept option (a) as a broad generalisation, not knowing Mahanadi and Godavari are specifically classified as surplus.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Mahanadi and Godavari — both peninsular rivers — are identified as surplus basins; the claim that all southern rivers are deficit is factually wrong.
Eliminate (b): Brahmaputra has the largest surplus in India — it is not a deficit basin; this is a geographic-swap error.
Eliminate (c): Surplus/deficit classification under NWDA is not purely seasonal — the 75% dependability criterion accounts for multi-year variability, not just monsoon vs. lean season.

Confirm (d): NWDA's surplus-deficit designation is season-specific and year-specific in practice — the static model does not capture the dynamic nature of surpluses that shift between monsoon and lean seasons.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is the primary scope-extension trap — the generalisation that 'all southern rivers are deficit' is a common but incorrect belief. Peninsular rivers like Mahanadi and Godavari have substantial surpluses and are the donor rivers in the cascade. This misconception is specifically flagged as a UPSC trap in the source material. Students who have not drilled down into basin-specific NWDA classifications will accept option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding which basins are genuinely surplus and which are deficit is foundational to evaluating NRLP's design logic.

• Option (a): Incorrect — This is the classic misconception. Mahanadi and Godavari are large-discharge peninsular rivers identified as surplus. Cauvery is deficit. The 'all southern rivers are deficit' generalisation is false.
• Option (b): Incorrect — Brahmaputra has India's largest water surplus by volume. It is deficit in utilisable harnessed form (due to terrain and geopolitics), not in natural discharge terms.
• Option (c): Incorrect — The 75% dependability criterion does attempt to account for year-to-year variation. The actual critique is that the model is static (based on historical averages) and does not dynamically account for climate-change-induced variability.
• Option (d): Correct — The most technically valid criticism of the NWDA methodology is that surplus/deficit designations depend on the season and the year assessed. A basin may be surplus in the monsoon season but deficit in the lean season — making the binary classification misleading for year-round planning.

Value Addition:
• 'Utilisable water resources' ≠ 'total water availability' — a critical distinction in NWDA methodology.
• Cauvery, Pennar, and Sabarmati are identified as deficit; Mahanadi, Godavari, Brahmaputra are surplus.
• Climate change is increasingly making historical surplus projections unreliable.

solution.concept_anchor: Himalayan component links — Kosi-Mechi vs. other named links
solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Gandak-Yamuna' sounds plausible as both Gandak and Yamuna are Ganga tributaries in the region, and students may accept this pairing as a Himalayan component link without verifying it.
elimination_logic: Option (a): Ghaghara-Yamuna is listed as one of the Himalayan component links — this pair is correctly matched.
Wait — re-evaluate: Ghaghara-Yamuna is a real Himalayan component link; option (a) would be correctly matched. Check option (b).

Option (c): Gandak-Yamuna is NOT a listed Himalayan component link — the documented link is Gandak-Ganga; this is an entity-swap.

Kosi-Mechi specifically paired with Bihar flood moderation is the most precisely correct pair — select (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap in option (c) substitutes 'Yamuna' for 'Ganga' in the Gandak link. Both Gandak and Yamuna are rivers in the Ganga basin, so 'Gandak-Yamuna' sounds geographically plausible. The documented link is Gandak-Ganga. solution.final_explanation:
The Himalayan Rivers Development Component includes 14 links, each with specific origin-destination river pairings and objectives.

• Option (a) — Ghaghara-Yamuna: This is a correctly matched pair — it is indeed a Himalayan component link. However, the flood control objective is primarily associated with the Kosi system, not Ghaghara-Yamuna, making this a partially correct match.
• Option (b) — Kosi-Mechi linked to Bihar flood moderation: Correctly matched. The Kosi-Mechi link is designed to transfer Kosi's flood surplus westward and explicitly serves the dual objective of irrigation and flood moderation in Bihar.
• Option (c) — Gandak-Yamuna: Incorrectly matched. The documented Himalayan component link involving Gandak is Gandak-Ganga, not Gandak-Yamuna. This is an entity-swap distractor.
• Option (d) — Brahmaputra-Ganga: While Brahmaputra surplus diversion to the Ganga basin is a long-term concept, it is not listed as a specific named link within the 14 Himalayan component links in the same way as Kosi-Mechi or Gandak-Ganga.

Value Addition:
• Kosi is known as 'Bihar's Sorrow' due to its catastrophic annual flooding — making Kosi-Mechi a high-priority flood management intervention.
• The 14 Himalayan links also include Kosi-Ghaghra and Gandak-Ganga.
• Nepal's territorial involvement makes Kosi and Gandak links diplomatically sensitive.

solution.concept_anchor: NRLP concept vs individual link projects — synonymy trap
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both A and R are true and that NWDA's technical role is related to the project-level implementation may assume R causally explains A, selecting (a).
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? NRLP as a programme and individual link projects under it are distinct — NRLP is the overarching National Perspective Plan, while each link (e.g., Ken-Betwa, Par-Tapi-Narmada) is a separate project requiring individual approvals, EIAs, and state agreements — A is correct.

Step 2 — Is R correct? NWDA prepares DPRs for individual links but does NOT implement them — implementation is by state governments or designated agencies. However, the statement that NWDA 'only prepares DPRs and has no implementation role' is factually correct — R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R explain A? The distinction between NRLP-as-a-concept and individual link projects is a planning/administrative distinction, not caused by NWDA's limited implementation mandate. Even if NWDA had implementation powers, NRLP and individual link projects would remain conceptually distinct. R does not causally explain A.

Both A and R are correct but R does NOT explain A — correct option is (b). Wait — re-check: Is R the correct explanation? No. So the answer is (b)... but let me re-evaluate R: 'NWDA prepares DPRs for individual link projects and has no direct project implementation authority.' This is correct. Does it explain why NRLP as a concept differs from individual link projects? No — that distinction exists at the policy planning level regardless of NWDA's mandate. Final answer: (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The conceptual distinction between NRLP as an overarching programme and individual link projects under it is a precision test that the UPSC frequently sets.

Assertion (A) — Correct: The National River Linking Project (National Perspective Plan) is an umbrella programme comprising 30 link proposals. Each individual link — Ken-Betwa, Par-Tapi-Narmada, Damanganga-Pinjal — is a separate project requiring its own feasibility study, EIA, interstate agreement, and Cabinet approval. Treating NRLP and any individual link as synonymous is a conceptual error.

Reason (R) — Correct: NWDA prepares Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) and feasibility reports for individual links but has no implementation authority. Implementation responsibility rests with state governments and designated project authorities.

Causal link — Does NOT hold: NWDA's limited mandate (DPR preparation only) does not cause or explain why NRLP is conceptually distinct from individual link projects. That distinction exists in the policy architecture itself, independent of NWDA's institutional role. Two independently true facts without a causal connection.

Value Addition:
• Ken-Betwa is the only individual link to have received Cabinet approval (2021) — all others remain at DPR or feasibility stage.
• Each link requires separate environmental clearance — the Supreme Court's 2012 order explicitly mandated this.
• NRLP's National Perspective Plan was prepared in 1980 — it is not a law but a planning document.

solution.concept_anchor: Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956 — Article 262 basis
solution.strong_distractor: d — 'River Boards Act, 1956' is from the same year (1956) as ISRWD Act and relates to inter-state rivers — a strong temporal and thematic distractor.
elimination_logic: The blank requires the name of the legislation that operationalises Article 262 of the Constitution for adjudicating inter-state river water disputes.
Eliminate (a): The National Water Policy 2012 is a policy document, not a dispute adjudication statute.
Eliminate (c): The River Boards Act, 1956 enables river boards for development — it is not the dispute adjudication law and has never actually been invoked.
Eliminate (d): The Environment Protection Act, 1986 governs environmental regulation — unrelated to water dispute adjudication.
Confirm (b): The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 was enacted to operationalise Article 262 and provides for the constitution of tribunals to adjudicate interstate water disputes.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The River Boards Act, 1956 (option d) is a powerful distractor: it was enacted in the same year, it relates to inter-state rivers, and its name implies a dispute-resolution or governance function. In reality, it provides for advisory river boards — it has no dispute adjudication mechanism and has never been activated. Students who know 1956 is the correct year but confuse the two Acts from the same year will choose (d).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 262 of the Constitution provides the constitutional basis for inter-state water dispute adjudication, but it requires implementing legislation to be effective.

• Option (a) — National Water Policy, 2012: Incorrect — a policy document, not a statute; has no dispute adjudication function.
• Option (b) — Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956: Correct — this statute was enacted under Article 262 and provides for the constitution of tribunals (e.g., Cauvery Tribunal, Krishna Tribunal) to adjudicate disputes between states over inter-state river waters.
• Option (c) — Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974: Incorrect — this governs water quality and pollution control, not inter-state water allocation disputes.
• Option (d) — River Boards Act, 1956: Incorrect — same year as the correct answer but serves a different function (enabling river boards for advice on conservation and development). Critically, it has never been used to constitute any river board.

Value Addition:
• Article 262 bars the Supreme Court from hearing inter-state water disputes once a tribunal is constituted.
• Tribunal awards under the ISRWD Act have the force of an order of the Supreme Court.
• The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (1990) and Mahanadi Tribunal (2018) are recent examples.
